lead.title: Four habits behind every platform I run.
lead.intro: Titles change. These don't. Each one comes with the work that proves it.

principles.label: Ownership
principles.title: I own what I run, including when it breaks.
principles.proof: At Sportserve I took over the CRM activation platform at handover and stood up its pre-production environment for six markets. When records went missing, I designed the Firestore-to-BigQuery backfill that brought them back.

principles.label: Delivery
principles.title: Investigation to production, then hand it over.
principles.proof: I took a server-side GTM marketing-campaign integration from first investigation to production in about five weeks, then documented it and handed the knowledge to the team so it doesn't depend on me.

principles.label: Partnership
principles.title: I sit between the business question and the pipeline.
principles.proof: I work with business analysts on payments intelligence, building the BigQuery tables and monitoring views behind affiliate statistics, bank-transaction matching and payment-provider reconciliation.

principles.label: Governance
principles.title: Trust is designed in, not bolted on.
principles.proof: As data architect across 20+ source systems, I built data-quality checks, master data management, PII/PHI masking and role-based access into the architecture from the first layer, not after the first audit.

cases.title: Three platforms, start to finish.
cases.intro: Pick one. Each opens on the problem, what I built, and what it changed.

items.title: Payment events, streamed to marketing in near real time.
items.problem: Marketing needed to see successful deposits as they happened, with the player and currency attached, and the team needed proof of every event that failed.
did: Built server-side tracking that streams successful-deposit events from the payments pipeline to GA4 through Google Tag Manager.
Attached player-level user IDs and a currency dimension, and logged every success and failure to BigQuery.
Took the server-side GTM campaign integration from investigation to production, then extended it toward first-time-deposit tracking.
items.result: Deposits reach GA4 with the player and currency on them, and every event, sent or failed, has a record in BigQuery.

metrics.label: in production, extending to first-time deposits

items.title: From on-premise servers to a governed cloud lakehouse.
items.problem: Enterprise data sat on on-premise systems that couldn't scale and couldn't feed the predictive work the business wanted.
did: Led the move to Databricks and Snowflake on a Medallion lakehouse: Bronze, Silver, Gold.
Governed it with Unity Catalog and packaged pipelines as modular Python wheels on YAML schedules.
Built PySpark feature engineering behind XGBoost, Random Forest and TFT models.
items.result: Enterprise data moved onto a governed cloud lakehouse, with Gold tables feeding three predictive model families.

metrics.label: Medallion layers, governed end to end

items.title: Twenty source systems, one warehouse people trust.
items.problem: More than twenty source systems, each shaped differently, and reporting that nobody fully trusted.
did: Reverse-engineered 40+ schemas and moved 15+ source systems into a Snowflake enterprise warehouse.
Unified 10+ systems into one Common Information Model, then designed the layers: raw, integration, Data Vault, dimensional, reporting.
Built in data-quality checks, MDM, PII/PHI masking and role-based access from the first layer.
items.result: More accurate, more trusted reporting on one architecture and one information model, with quality and access rules enforced by the platform instead of by hand.

contact.intro: If you’re building a data platform that has to be right and has to be fast, I’d like to hear about it.
contact.availability: Based in Nairobi, working with teams across time zones.
